title: Divorce
description: The American society drama: a divorce case and the double standard. It is a dramatic work of 1871 by Augustin Daly; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Sensation Drama and the Domestic Stage.
plot_or_argument: A fashionable wife discovers her husband's infidelity and sues for divorce; the play follows the case, the scandal and the reconciliation through the drawing rooms and the courtroom, in the most successful American society drama of the 1870s.
narrative_structure: Five acts, from the discovery to the trial and the reconciliation. The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
principal_characters: the wife; the husband; the lover; the lawyer; the fashionable world
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the well-made adaptation of the European play.
historical_context: New York in the 1870s, the fashionable world and the American divorce courts. The record dates the work as composed between 1870 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; sensation drama and the domestic stage.
literary_significance: Divorce was the most successful American society drama of the 1870s: its treatment of the double standard made it a scandal and a success, and it established Daly as the leading manager of the American stage.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as John Augustin Daly. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1871, as play (five acts), by Augustin Daly. Composed between 1870 and 1871. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: A History of Nineteenth Century Literature
description: The central academic history of Victorian literature: the survey and the judgement. It is a prose work of 1896 by George Saintsbury; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Saintsbury surveys the literature of the nineteenth century from the Romantic poets to the Victorians, with chapters on the novel, the drama, the essay and the historians, and with judgements that made and unmade reputations.
narrative_structure: A literary history in chapters by genre and author. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
principal_characters: Saintsbury as critic; the poets; the novelists; the historians
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the survey history with its judgements.
historical_context: Britain in the 1890s, the new academic study of English literature and the literary establishment. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
literary_significance: A History of Nineteenth Century Literature is the central academic history of Victorian literature and the book that established English literature as a university subject: Saintsbury's survey and his judgements made him the most influential critic of the period.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as George Edward Bateman Saintsbury. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1896, as prose (literary history), by George Saintsbury. Composed between 1894 and 1896. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Methods of Ethics
description: The greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century: the analysis of the methods of ethics. It is a prose work of 1874 by Henry Sidgwick; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Sidgwick examines the three methods by which we reason about conduct — egoism, intuitionism and utilitarianism — and shows that they cannot be reconciled without a further postulate, in an analysis that made him the central moral philosopher of the age.
narrative_structure: Four books of philosophical analysis. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Sidgwick as philosopher; the egoist; the intuitionist; the utilitarian
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the analytical survey of the competing methods of ethics.
historical_context: Cambridge in the 1870s, the utilitarian tradition and the crisis of Victorian religious belief. The record dates the work as composed between 1873 and 1874 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Methods of Ethics is the greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century and the foundation of modern utilitarian ethics: its rigorous analysis of the conflict between self-interest and the general good made it the central text of Victorian moral philosophy.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. Sidgwick. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1874, as prose (moral philosophy), by Henry Sidgwick. Composed between 1873 and 1874. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: A History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne
alternative_titles: History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne
description: The great rationalist history of the Victorian age: the rise of morals and the decline of superstition. It is a prose work of 1869 by William Lecky; it belongs to Arnold and the Criticism of Culture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Lecky traces the moral history of Europe from the Roman Empire to Charlemagne: the pagan virtues, the rise of Christianity, the monastic ideal, the treatment of women and slaves, and the growth of the moral sense, in a history written from a rationalist and liberal standpoint.
narrative_structure: A history in two volumes, from Augustus to Charlemagne. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Lecky as historian; the Roman moralists; the Christian fathers; the barbarian kings
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is the historical survey of opinion and morals.
historical_context: Europe in the first eight centuries, and the Victorian controversy over the history of Christianity. The record dates the work as composed between 1866 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: A History of European Morals was the great rationalist history of the Victorian age: it made Lecky the central historian of modern unbelief, influenced Mill, Stephen and the whole liberal intelligentsia, and remains the founding text of the secular history of morals.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Edward Hartpole Lecky. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1869, as prose (history of morals), by William Lecky. Composed between 1866 and 1869. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Across Patagonia
description: A woman's narrative of a riding and hunting expedition across southern Patagonia in 1878-79. It is a prose work of 1880 by Lady Florence Dixie; it is catalogued here under Imperial Adventure Romance; Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait.
plot_or_argument: Weary of English society, the narrator sails for the Strait of Magellan with her husband, two of her brothers and Julius Beerbohm, who acts as guide. From Punta Arenas the party rides north across the pampas towards the Cordillera with horses, hunting dogs and hired guides, living on the guanaco and ostrich it shoots, visiting an Indian encampment and being overtaken by a prairie fire in which her horse bolts with her. Throughout, the narrator hunts and endures hardship on equal terms with the men, and she rarely names her husband.
narrative_structure: A book-length first-person narrative in chapters, following the expedition in the order of the journey from the voyage out to the ride across the pampas, with illustrations.
principal_characters: the narrator (Lady Florence Dixie); her husband; her brothers Lord Queensberry and Lord James Douglas; Julius Beerbohm, the guide; the hired guides
meter_and_prosody: Prose: a plain, vigorous first-person narrative of riding, camping and the hunt, alternating with Romantic set pieces of landscape and weather.
historical_context: The expedition, begun two months after the birth of her second son, was in her own words an escape from 'civilization and its surroundings'; the book appeared in 1880, before her South African despatches, and she sent a copy to Charles Darwin with a correction of his account of the tuco-tuco, which she had seen abroad by day.
literary_significance: Across Patagonia made Dixie's name: its narrator rides, hunts and endures on equal terms with the men of her party, and its self-portrait of an active, resilient woman in a wild country, set against the Victorian ideal of female fragility, anticipates the feminist argument of her later fiction.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Florence Caroline Douglas. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1880, as travel narrative, by Lady Florence Dixie. Composed between 1879 and 1880. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Gloriana; or, The Revolution of 1900
description: A feminist utopian novel in which a woman, disguised as a man, becomes Prime Minister and wins the vote for women. It is a prose fiction work of 1890 by Lady Florence Dixie; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
plot_or_argument: As a girl Gloria de Lara vows to free her sex; disguised as Hector D'Estrange she passes through Eton and Oxford, founds institutions where women learn to ride, shoot and swim, and enters the House of Commons, where her campaign makes women's suffrage law and, at twenty-eight, wins her the premiership. Lord Westray, the man who had wronged her mother, hides himself so that D'Estrange is tried for his murder; at the trial D'Estrange confesses that he is a woman, Gloria de Lara, and is sentenced, but Flora Desmond and her White Guards rescue her and she escapes her pursuers. The disclosure wins many waverers to her side, a general election returns her party with a majority over all the others, and a closing chapter set in 1999 describes a prosperous and peaceful Britain transformed by women's share in its government.
narrative_structure: A polemical preface followed by a novel in three books of short chapters, narrated largely in the present tense and ending in a chapter set in 1999.
principal_characters: Gloria de Lara (Hector D'Estrange); Mrs de Lara, her mother; Captain Kintore, her father; Lord Westray; Flora Desmond and her White Guards; Colonel Delamere
meter_and_prosody: Prose: a declamatory present-tense narrative of melodrama and political oratory, with set-piece speeches in Parliament and the courtroom and occasional verse.
historical_context: Published by Henry and Co. in 1890, while women's suffrage bills were repeatedly failing in the Commons; Dixie's preface argues not only for the vote but for educating the sexes together and opening every profession and position to women.
literary_significance: Gloriana turned the suffrage argument into utopian romance: its heroine wins the vote for women by passing as a man and governing as Prime Minister, is vindicated when her sex is revealed, and is surrounded by women who drive the plot, so that the novel joins the feminist utopia to romance, trial melodrama and detective plotting.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Florence Caroline Douglas. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1890, as novel, by Lady Florence Dixie. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Sartor Resartus: The Life and Opinions of Herr Teufelsdröckh
description: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine in 1833-34 and published as a book in Boston in 1836 and in London in 1838: a 'clothes philosophy' in the form of an English editor's account of the German professor Diogenes Teufelsdröckh and his book on clothes, which becomes the spiritual autobiography of a modern soul.
plot_or_argument: The editor presents Teufelsdröckh's life and his 'Philosophy of Clothes', the doctrine that all institutions, creeds and customs are garments which time wears out. Teufelsdröckh's own history — the 'Everlasting No' of his despair, the 'Centre of Indifference', and the 'Everlasting Yea' of work and renunciation — is the model of the Victorian conversion narrative.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Diogenes Teufelsdröckh; the English editor; Hofrath Heuschrecke; Blumine; Herr Towgood; Gretchen
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: German idealist philosophy (Fichte, Goethe, Kant) and the Scottish Calvinist background; the crisis of faith of the 1820s; and the Fraser's Magazine circle of the 1830s. The record dates the work as composed between 1833 and 1834 and first published in 1836 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Sartor Resartus introduced German idealism to English readers and invented the modern spiritual autobiography of doubt and recovery; it was the single greatest influence on the Victorian literature of the 'Everlasting No', and Emerson's American edition of 1836 made Carlyle the intellectual hero of New England Transcendentalism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine from November 1833 to August 1834 in ten instalments, interrupted by reader protest; the first book edition was issued at Boston by James Munroe in 1836 with an introduction by Ralph Waldo Emerson, and the first English edition by Chapman and Hall in 1838. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The French Revolution: A History
description: Published in three volumes in 1837 after the manuscript of the first volume was accidentally burned by John Stuart Mill's housemaid: the greatest work of Victorian historiography and the book that made Carlyle famous.
plot_or_argument: The three parts — 'The Bastille', 'The Constitution', 'The Guillotine' — narrate the French Revolution from the death of Louis XV to the fall of Robespierre, by a method of vivid present-tense scenes, documents, portraits and choric commentary rather than by continuous analysis; the Revolution is presented as a terrible and necessary judgment on a corrupt society.
narrative_structure: Three parts of seven, five and seven books, in a loosely chronological sequence of scenes and portraits rather than an analytical argument.
literary_form: Historical prose narrative in three parts
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The 1830s and the memory of 1789 and 1830; Carlyle's reading of the French memoirs and pamphlets; and the British debate on reform that made the French Revolution a living political question. The record dates the work as composed between 1834 and 1837 and first published in 1837 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The French Revolution changed the writing of history in English: its present-tense scenes, its documentary collage and its prophetic judgement created the modern literary history. Dickens used it as a source for A Tale of Two Cities, and its account of the Revolution as the work of 'the great dumb deep' shaped the Victorian and modern understanding of revolutionary politics.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1837, as historical prose narrative in three parts, by Thomas Carlyle. Composed between 1834 and 1837. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
description: Six lectures delivered in London in May 1840 and published in 1841: the most influential Victorian statement of the theory that history is the biography of great men, organised as six types of hero — the divinity (Odin), the prophet (Muhammad), the poet (Dante, Shakespeare), the priest (Luther, Knox), the man of letters (Johnson, Rousseau, Burns) and the king (Cromwell, Napoleon).
plot_or_argument: Each lecture presents its hero as the 'sincere' man who perceives the truth of his age and embodies it in action, and the sequence is an argument that the modern age, having lost its faith, finds its heroes in literature and in the 'man of letters'.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The 1840 lecture season, the Chartist agitation of 1839-40, and the Victorian search for authority after the collapse of the old order; the lectures were attended by Dickens, Mill and the intellectual public of London.
literary_significance: On Heroes made hero-worship a central Victorian idea and supplied the age's theory of leadership; it shaped Carlyle's own Cromwell and Frederick, and Emerson's Representative Men, and its account of the man of letters as the modern priest gave Victorian authorship its sense of vocation. The twentieth century's reaction against its authoritarian implications made it the classic text for the critique of Victorian political thought.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1841, as six lectures (delivered May 1840; published 1841), by Thomas Carlyle. Composed in 1840. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Past and Present
description: Written in seven weeks in 1843 and the most concentrated of Carlyle's social criticisms: a comparison of the twelfth-century monastery of Bury St Edmunds, recovered from the chronicle of Jocelin of Brakelond, with the 'condition of England' in the Hungry Forties.
plot_or_argument: Book I, 'Proem', states the diagnosis of a society without a soul; Book II, 'The Ancient Monk', narrates Abbot Samson's governance of the monastery as a model of work and order; Book III, 'The Modern Worker', presents the 'Manchester insurrection', the 'Gospel of Work' and the parson and the priest of the modern world; Book IV, 'Horoscope', prophesies the consequences of the neglect of the poor.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The Chartist riots of 1839-42, the 'Hungry Forties', the New Poor Law and the factory system, and the Victorian debate between laissez-faire and the duty of the state. The record dates the work as composed in 1843 and first published in 1843 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
literary_significance: Past and Present is the founding text of Victorian social criticism and the source of much of the vocabulary of the later Labour movement; its 'Gospel of Work', its attack on the 'cash nexus' and its demand for a governing aristocracy of talent shaped Ruskin, Dickens, Kingsley, Morris and the Christian socialists, and it remains the classic English indictment of industrial capitalism from the right.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Chapman and Hall in April 1843. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Chartism
description: Published in December 1839 at the height of the Chartist agitation and the most important contemporary analysis of it by an intellectual: an essay that takes the Charter seriously as a symptom of a deeper condition rather than as a programme.
plot_or_argument: Carlyle asks 'what the condition of England really is' and answers that Chartism is the symptom of the 'dyspepsia' of a society in which the working man has no voice, no leader and no hope; the remedy is not the ballot but the recognition of the duties of the governing class and the right of the worker to work.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a pamphlet, a single argument in a short compass. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The Chartist petition of 1839, the Newport rising of November 1839, the Poor Law and the factory question; Carlyle's argument was delivered as the agitation reached its height. The record dates the work as composed in 1839 and first published in 1840 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Chartism invented the phrase 'the condition of England question' and set the terms of the Victorian social novel: Disraeli's Sybil, Gaskell's Mary Barton and Dickens's Hard Times all answer Carlyle's diagnosis, and it is the founding document of the critique of Victorian industrialism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Houlston and Stoneman in December 1839, expanding the Westminster Review article of January 1839. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches: with Elucidations
description: Published in 1845, and the work that rehabilitated Cromwell in the English historical imagination: the letters and speeches, edited with a commentary that presents Cromwell as the sincere Puritan hero and the founder of English liberty.
plot_or_argument: Carlyle arranges the documents chronologically from the 1620s to Cromwell's death in 1658, with 'elucidations' that supply narrative and argument; the effect is a first-person portrait of the man in his own words, from the fen drainage and the Irish campaign to the Protectorate and the deathbed.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The 1840s and the Victorian interest in the Puritan past, the edition of the letters by Carlyle's friend Thomas Carlyle and the earlier editions of the Thurloe papers, and the 1841-42 controversy over Cromwell's statue.
literary_significance: Cromwell's Letters and Speeches made Cromwell a Victorian hero and established the documentary edition as a form of historical writing; it shaped Froude's and Gardiner's histories and the modern scholarly edition, and it is the classic example of Carlyle's method of letting a man speak for himself.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1845, as documentary edition with commentary, by Thomas Carlyle. Composed between 1844 and 1845. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Life of John Sterling
description: Published in 1851, Carlyle's brief and moving biography of his friend John Sterling, the Irish-born writer and clergyman who moved from Coleridgean idealism through the Oxford Movement to a free-thinking Christianity and died at forty.
plot_or_argument: Carlyle follows Sterling's life from Cambridge and the Apostles through his marriage, his colonial venture in the West Indies, his editorship of the Athenaeum, his friendship with Carlyle and his final years of illness and religious searching, quoting the letters and setting them in the narrative.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: John Sterling; Thomas Carlyle, the narrator; Edward Sterling, his father; Frederick Denison Maurice; Samuel Taylor Coleridge; Julius Hare
literary_form: Biography; review essay, first issued in 1851
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s, the Oxford Movement, the Athenaeum, and the Victorian crisis of faith as it appeared in an individual life. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Life of John Sterling is the finest of Carlyle's shorter biographies and a central document of Victorian friendship and religious doubt; it is also the model for the Victorian life-and-letters biography that Gaskell's Brontë and Froude's Carlyle later practised.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Chapman and Hall in April 1851. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: History of Friedrich II of Prussia, called Frederick the Great
description: Published in six volumes between 1858 and 1865, the last and longest of Carlyle's works, and the most ambitious Victorian attempt to write the history of an age through the biography of a king. It is a prose work of 1858 by Thomas Carlyle; it belongs to Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The history follows Frederick from his brutal upbringing under Frederick William I through the Silesian wars, the Seven Years' War and the partition of Poland to his death in 1786, with long digressions on the German princes, the Prussian army and the diplomacy of the eighteenth century.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences.
historical_context: The 1850s-60s, the Crimean War and the rise of Prussia, and the Victorian admiration for German culture and efficiency. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1865 and first published in 1858 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Frederick the Great is Carlyle's masterpiece of narrative history and one of the great monuments of Victorian prose; it made the eighteenth century live for English readers and established the narrative-history method that Macaulay and Froude practised, and its admiration for Prussian order shaped Victorian and later attitudes to Germany.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1858, as historical narrative in six volumes, by Thomas Carlyle. Composed between 1851 and 1865. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Modern Painters
alternative_titles: Modern Painters: Their Superiority in the Art of Landscape Painting
description: Begun in 1843 as a defence of J. M. W. Turner under the anonymous title 'by a Graduate of Oxford' and completed in 1860 in five volumes: the most ambitious work of art criticism in English, moving from the truth of landscape painting to a complete theory of the imagination and of the relation of art to religion.
plot_or_argument: Volume I defends Turner's truth to nature against the critics; Volume II (1846) develops the theory of the beautiful and the 'pathetic fallacy' and the classification of the 'theoretic' and 'imaginative' faculties; Volumes III-V (1856-60) treat the symbolism of landscape, the Renaissance and the relation of art to the moral and religious state of the artist's age.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
historical_context: The 1840s and the Turner controversy, the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of 1848 (which Ruskin defended in 1851), the growth of the Victorian art market, and Ruskin's own travels in Italy and Switzerland.
literary_significance: Modern Painters established Ruskin as the leading art critic of the century and made Turner a national painter; it introduced the 'pathetic fallacy' into criticism, gave the Pre-Raphaelites their critical defence, and turned art criticism into a branch of moral philosophy that Pater and Wilde had to answer.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Volume I was published by Smith, Elder in May 1843 by 'a Graduate of Oxford' and carried no author's name; the five volumes appeared in 1843, 1846, 1851, 1856 and 1860. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Seven Lamps of Architecture
description: Published in 1849 with Ruskin's own etchings, and the first statement of the moral theory of architecture: the seven lamps of Sacrifice, Truth, Power, Beauty, Life, Memory and Obedience. It is a prose work of 1849 by John Ruskin; it belongs to Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Each lamp is a principle tested against buildings old and new; the lamp of Truth condemns the imitation of materials and the restoration of ancient buildings; the lamp of Memory makes buildings the record of a nation's past; the lamp of Obedience argues for the authority of tradition in architecture.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
historical_context: The Victorian Gothic Revival, the restoration controversies of the 1840s (the 'Anti-Scrape' campaign Ruskin later supported), and the railway and industrial building of the period. The record dates the work as composed in 1848 and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The Seven Lamps founded the moral criticism of architecture and the Victorian Gothic Revival's intellectual programme; its attack on restoration led directly to William Morris's Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (1877), and its seven principles became the vocabulary of the Arts and Crafts movement.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Smith, Elder in May 1849, with etched plates by the author. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Stones of Venice
description: Published in three volumes between 1851 and 1853 and the central work of Ruskin's middle period: a history of Venetian architecture and a moral history of the Venetian republic that becomes, in the chapter 'The Nature of Gothic', a criticism of industrial labour.
plot_or_argument: Volume I treats the foundations and the Byzantine style, Volume II the Gothic palaces and the 'Nature of Gothic' chapter, Volume III the Renaissance and the fall of Venice; the argument is that the decline of Venetian architecture follows the decline of Venetian faith and that the workers of the Gothic cathedral were free men while those of the Renaissance were slaves.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
literary_form: Architectural and social criticism in three volumes
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
historical_context: The 1848 revolutions and the siege of Venice, the Victorian Gothic Revival, and the pre-Raphaelite critique of industrial labour; the book was read by Morris at Oxford in 1853 and changed his life. The record dates the work as composed between 1849 and 1853 and first published in 1851 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The Stones of Venice is the founding text of the social criticism of art: 'The Nature of Gothic' gave Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement their central doctrine that good art depends on the free labour of the craftsman, and through Morris it shaped the socialism of the 1880s and the twentieth-century theory of design.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Smith, Elder in three volumes: Volume I (The Foundations) in April 1851, Volume II (The Sea-Stories) in July 1853 and Volume III (The Fall) in June 1853, with plates drawn and engraved by the author. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Unto This Last: Four Essays on the First Principles of Political Economy
description: Four essays published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1860 under the title 'Unto This Last' (the parable of the labourers in the vineyard) and collected as a book in 1862: the most influential attack on classical political economy in English.
plot_or_argument: Ruskin argues that the 'economic man' of Ricardo and Mill is a fiction, that wealth is not the accumulation of commodities but the possession of 'things that are useful and life-giving', that the 'illth' produced by commerce is a real cost, and that the just wage and the responsibility of the employer are moral duties. He proposes a guild of labourers and an education for the poor.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
historical_context: The 1860 Cornhill controversy (Thackeray, the editor, stopped the series after the fourth essay), the Lancashire cotton famine of 1861-65, and the socialist and Christian-socialist movements of the 1880s.
literary_significance: Unto This Last is the most influential English work of moral economics: Gandhi read it in 1904 and said it 'captured' him and led him to the doctrine of the 'welfare of all'; Attlee and the founders of the British Labour Party took their moral vocabulary from it, and it is the founding text of the twentieth-century critique of economics as a value-free science.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Smith, Elder in May 1862; the four essays had appeared in The Cornhill Magazine in 1860 and their withdrawal under pressure was one of the events of Victorian periodical history. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Sesame and Lilies
description: Two lectures delivered in Manchester and Dublin in 1864 and published in 1865: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' on reading and education, and 'Of Queens' Gardens' on the education of women, the most widely read of all Ruskin's writings.
plot_or_argument: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' argues that true reading is an act of attention and obedience to the author, and that a nation's education consists in its libraries and its reading; 'Of Queens' Gardens' argues that women should be educated to a 'queenly' influence in the home, and its conservative ideal of womanhood provoked a long controversy.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
historical_context: The 1860s, the movement for women's higher education (Girton, 1869; Newnham, 1871), and Ruskin's own lectures at the Working Men's College. The record dates the work as composed in 1864 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: Sesame and Lilies was the most widely read of Ruskin's books and the one that made him a public educator; 'Of Queens' Gardens' became a central text in the Victorian debate on women's education, and its ideal of 'queenly' domesticity was the target of the New Woman argument of the 1890s. The essays are the classic English statements of the moral value of reading.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Smith, Elder in June 1865, collecting the 1864 Manchester lectures 'Of Kings' Treasuries' and 'Of Queens' Gardens'. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Praeterita: Outlines of Scenes and Thoughts Perhaps Worthy of Memory in My Past Life
description: Ruskin's autobiography, serialised in the magazine of the same name in twenty-four parts from 1885 and left unfinished in 1889: the most beautiful of Victorian autobiographies, and the retrospective re-creation of a childhood, a family and a Europe before the railway.
plot_or_argument: The narrative moves from the London house of his childhood and the sherry business of his father to the Continental tours of 1833-1845, his mother and father, his boyish passion for Adèle Domecq (his marriage to Effie Gray is passed over in silence), his work on Modern Painters and the Stones of Venice, and the death of his parents; the last chapters are fragmentary and haunted.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
principal_characters: John Ruskin, the narrator; John James Ruskin, his father; Margaret Ruskin, his mother; Adèle Domecq; Rose La Touche; Joan Severn
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is precise, patient description of natural fact.
historical_context: The 1880s, Ruskin's failing mind and the death of his parents, and the Victorian vogue for autobiography (Mill, Darwin, Trollope, Newman). The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Ruskin and the Political Economy of Art; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: Praeterita is the finest Victorian autobiography after Mill's and the model for the twentieth-century literary memoir; its reconstruction of childhood perception and its refusal of the conventional pieties made it a central text for Pater, Proust and the modern autobiography, and its unfinished condition is itself a document of the age.
attribution_notes: Unfinished: Ruskin wrote twenty-four chapters of a projected longer work and abandoned it in 1889 as his mental health failed; the published text is what he left.
bibliographical_notes: Published in instalments by George Allen from 1885 to 1889 and left unfinished at the author's death; it is the autobiography written in the intervals of madness. The research status is partial. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
alternative_titles: System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
description: Published in 1843 and the foundational work of English empiricist philosophy of science: an account of the methods of induction, of the logic of the moral sciences, and of the errors of the a priori school.
plot_or_argument: The six books treat names and propositions, reasoning, induction, the operations subsidiary to induction, the fallacies, and the logic of the moral sciences. The central contribution is the formulation of the 'methods of experimental inquiry' — agreement, difference, residues and concomitant variations — and the argument that the moral sciences must be deductive in method but cannot predict individual conduct.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s, the Scottish philosophy of Thomas Brown and Dugald Stewart, Whewell's and Herschel's philosophy of science, and the controversy with the intuitionist school of Coleridge and Hamilton. The record dates the work as composed between 1830 and 1843 and first published in 1843 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The System of Logic established the empiricist philosophy of science in English and gave the social sciences their methodological foundation; its 'methods of inquiry' are still the standard formulation, and its sixth book founded the modern logic of the social sciences.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. S. Mill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1843, as philosophical treatise in six books, by John Stuart Mill. Composed between 1830 and 1843. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Principles of Political Economy, with Some of Their Applications to Social Philosophy
description: Published in 1848 and the standard English economics text for a generation: a systematic restatement of the classical political economy that opened the way for reform by distinguishing the laws of production from the arrangements of distribution.
plot_or_argument: The five books treat production, distribution (property, wages, profits, rent), exchange (value, money, international trade), the progress of society, and the influence of government, including the case for the taxation of unearned increments, the reform of land tenure, and the stationary state as a possible good rather than a disaster.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
historical_context: The 1847 crisis and the Irish famine, the Chartist and cooperative movements, the land question, and the socialist criticisms of Louis Blanc and the English Owenites. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1848 and first published in 1848 and the corpus places it within Carlyle and the Hero-Worship Lecture; Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
literary_significance: The Principles taught political economy to the English-speaking world (the first edition sold out in a year) and made the distinction between production and distribution the basis of the reformist economics that led to the welfare state; Mill's discussion of the stationary state and the environment is the founding text of ecological economics.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. S. Mill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1848, as economic treatise in five books, by John Stuart Mill. Composed between 1845 and 1848. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: On Liberty
description: Published in 1859 with the dedication to Harriet Taylor Mill, and the single most influential defence of individual freedom in the English language: the argument that the only justification for coercing an individual is to prevent harm to others.
plot_or_argument: The five chapters treat the history of liberty and the tyranny of opinion, the liberty of thought and discussion, individuality as one of the elements of well-being, the limits of the authority of society over the individual, and applications of the doctrine to education and the state.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
historical_context: The 1850s, the growth of Victorian public opinion and the 'despotism of custom', the temperance and sabbatarian legislation, and Mill's own collaboration with Harriet Taylor. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: On Liberty gave liberalism its central principle and its most quoted defence of free speech ('If all mankind minus one were of one opinion...'); it is a foundation text of modern democratic theory and civil liberties law, and it remains the reference point for the debate on the limits of state action.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. S. Mill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by John W. Parker and Son in London in June 1859, one volume, dated 1859; the essay is dedicated to Harriet Taylor Mill and was written between 1854 and 1858. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Utilitarianism
description: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and published in 1863: the classic statement of the utilitarian ethics of the greatest happiness principle, with the influential distinction between higher and lower pleasures.
plot_or_argument: The five chapters treat the question of utility, the 'proof' of the principle (that the only evidence of desirability is actual desire), the ultimate sanction of the principle in the social feelings, the proof of the principle, and the connection between justice and utility.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
historical_context: The 1860s, the critique of utilitarianism by Whewell, Hamilton and Carlyle, and the social reform movements that Mill hoped to ground in a philosophical ethics. The record dates the work as composed in 1861 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Utilitarianism is the definitive formulation of the ethics that the Victorian age inherited from Bentham and Mill's father, and the higher/lower pleasures distinction gave modern moral philosophy one of its central arguments; the justice chapter is still the starting point for the modern debate on punishment and rights.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. S. Mill. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Parker, Son and Bourn in April 1863, having appeared in three parts in Fraser's Magazine in 1861. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Subjection of Women
description: Published in 1869, written in collaboration with Harriet Taylor and dedicated to her: the most rigorous philosophical argument for the equality of women in the nineteenth century, and the text that the Victorian women's movement took as its manifesto.
plot_or_argument: Mill argues that the subjection of women is a relic of the past preserved by custom, that the evidence of women's inferiority is worthless because it is drawn from a state of constrained development, that the legal ownership of wives under coverture is a form of slavery, that women should be enabled to choose any profession, and that marriage should become a partnership of equals.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose.
historical_context: The 1860s and the campaign for women's suffrage, the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882, and the parliamentary debate on the Second Reform Act in which Mill proposed the inclusion of women.
literary_significance: The Subjection of Women is the founding document of modern liberal feminism and remains the classic philosophical statement of the case: it gave the nineteenth-century women's movement its intellectual authority, and its analysis of the 'custom' and the 'nature' argument is still the core of the modern debate.
attribution_notes: Published under Mill's name; he states in the Autobiography and in the dedication that the book was an embodiment of his wife's ideas and the result of their collaboration, and modern scholarship (Hayek, Rose, and the Oxford edition) treats Harriet Taylor Mill's share as substantial.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Longmans, Green, Reader and Dyer in May 1869; the essay was written in 1861 and held back by its author until he judged the moment. The record grades the work as major canon.
